passages.text: Before electric refrigerators, many households in the northern United States relied on ice cut from frozen lakes in winter. Workers sawed the ice into large blocks, packed them in sawdust inside insulated icehouses, and sold the ice throughout the summer. By the mid-1800s, the trade had grown so large that ships carried New England ice as far as the Caribbean and India.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before refrigeration, cutting and storing natural ice was a large industry that supplied ice through the summer and even overseas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sawdust was the most effective insulating material available in the 1800s.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most of the ice shipped from New England melted before it reached India.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electric refrigerators were invented because the ice trade could not meet demand.

content.explanation: The text describes how ice was harvested and stored so it could be sold all summer, then stresses how big the trade became, reaching the Caribbean and India. Choice A captures both points.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Sawdust is one detail of how ice was stored; the text doesn't compare it with other materials.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says nothing about how much ice melted on the way.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text doesn't explain why refrigerators were invented.

passages.text: Tardigrades, microscopic animals often called water bears, are famous for surviving conditions that would kill most living things. When their surroundings dry out, they pull in their legs, lose nearly all of their body water and enter a dormant state. In this form, some tardigrades have survived extreme cold, high doses of radiation and even several days of exposure to outer space.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tardigrades are the smallest animals known to science.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some tardigrades live permanently in outer space.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tardigrades can survive extreme conditions, largely by entering a dried-out, dormant state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scientists study tardigrades mainly to develop new treatments for radiation exposure.

content.explanation: The first sentence states that tardigrades survive conditions that kill most living things. The rest explains how (a dried-out dormant state) and lists examples of what they survive. Choice C sums this up.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text calls tardigrades microscopic but never says they are the smallest animals.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says some survived several days of exposure to space, not that they live there.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text doesn't say why scientists study tardigrades.

passages.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published an English translation of an article about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a proposed calculating machine that was never completed. The notes she added were roughly three times as long as the article itself. In them, she laid out a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate a series of numbers and suggested that such a machine might one day work with symbols other than numbers, perhaps even composing music.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lovelace helped Babbage finish building the Analytical Engine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lovelace's most important contribution was translating Babbage's ideas accurately into English.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lovelace used the Analytical Engine to compose music.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lovelace's notes went far beyond a translation, offering both a detailed procedure for the machine and a broad vision of what such machines could do.

content.explanation: The text stresses that Lovelace's notes were much longer than the article and describes what was in them: a step-by-step method for calculating and the idea that machines could work with symbols such as music. Choice D captures this.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says the Analytical Engine was never completed.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The translation is mentioned, but the text emphasizes her added notes, which went well beyond translating.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Lovelace only suggested that such a machine might someday compose music; the engine was never built.

passages.text: Ecologist Marisol Quintero wanted to know why a certain wildflower grows densely along hiking trails but sparsely in nearby meadows. She first suspected that hikers' boots were carrying its seeds, but seed counts in trailside soil and in meadow soil turned out to be similar. She then found that the trailside soil, packed down by foot traffic, held moisture longer after rain, and that the flower's seedlings survived far better in moist soil.

content.stem: According to the text, what led Quintero to reject her first explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trailside soil held moisture longer after rain than meadow soil did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The flower's seedlings survived better in moist soil.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seed counts were similar in trailside soil and meadow soil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hikers rarely stepped off the trails into the meadows.

content.explanation: Quintero first thought boots carried seeds to the trails, which would mean more seeds there. But seed counts were similar in both places, so extra seeds couldn't explain the difference. That finding (choice C) is what ruled out her first idea.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This finding supports her second explanation; it isn't why she dropped the first one.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This also supports the second explanation about soil moisture.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says nothing about where hikers stepped.

passages.text: Folklorists have long noted that in many traditional tales, a task is attempted three times, often by three siblings, and only the third attempt succeeds. Scholar Eamon Pryce argues that this pattern is not merely decorative. In stories passed down by word of mouth, he notes, repetition helps listeners keep track of the plot, and the first two failures establish what is at stake, so the third attempt carries more suspense.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pryce argues that the pattern of three attempts in traditional tales serves both practical and dramatic purposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In traditional tales, the youngest of three siblings is always the one who succeeds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Written versions of traditional tales have abandoned the pattern of three attempts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folklorists disagree about how many traditional tales use the pattern of three attempts.

content.explanation: After introducing the pattern, the text presents Pryce's argument that it "is not merely decorative": repetition helps listeners remember (a practical purpose) and the failures build suspense (a dramatic purpose). Choice A sums up that argument.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says the attempts are "often" by three siblings and doesn't say the youngest always succeeds; this overstates the text.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text doesn't discuss written versions of the tales.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says folklorists "have long noted" the pattern; it describes no disagreement about it.

passages.text: When a new variety of millet that produced larger harvests was introduced in one farming region, agricultural economist Jonas Ekberg expected farmers to adopt it quickly. Many did not. Interviews revealed that the new variety yielded more in good years but failed badly in droughts, while the traditional variety produced smaller but more dependable harvests. For families with no savings to fall back on, Ekberg concluded, avoiding a disastrous year mattered more than raising the average harvest.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new millet variety produced smaller harvests than the traditional variety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Farmers' reluctance to adopt the new variety reflected a reasonable preference for reliable harvests over higher average ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Farmers in the region were unaware that a new millet variety was available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ekberg recommends that the new millet variety be withdrawn from the region.

content.explanation: The text explains why many farmers didn't switch: the new millet yields more on average but fails in droughts, and families without savings can't risk a disastrous year. Choice B states this central point.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says the new variety produced larger harvests in good years.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The farmers' choice was based on how the varieties performed, which implies they knew about the new one.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Ekberg explains the farmers' choice; he doesn't recommend withdrawing the variety.

passages.text: Every Sunday, Theo's grandfather fixed something in the house that was not broken. He tightened hinges that did not squeak, oiled a clock that kept perfect time and replaced a light bulb that had months of life left in it. Once, Theo asked him why. His grandfather looked at the clock for a long moment before answering. "Your grandmother used to give me a list," he said, and went back to work.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theo's grandfather is a skilled craftsman who takes pride in keeping the house in perfect condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theo is frustrated that his grandfather wastes his Sundays on unnecessary chores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theo's grandfather keeps up his Sunday repairs, though they are unneeded, as a way of holding on to a routine he once shared with his wife.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theo's grandfather worries that the house will fall apart if he stops working on it.

content.explanation: The repairs are clearly unnecessary: nothing he fixes is broken. When asked why, the grandfather pauses and explains that his wife "used to give me a list," which suggests she no longer does and that the Sunday repairs carry on a habit tied to her. Choice C captures this.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text shows he does repairs, but it emphasizes that they are unneeded and connects them to his wife, not to pride in his skill.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Theo asks a question, but nothing shows he is frustrated.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Everything he fixes already works, so the repairs aren't about preventing the house from falling apart.

passages.text: It is often said that the human brain is fully developed by early adulthood. Neuroscientist Hye-jin Park argues that this claim is misleading, less because of any single fact it gets wrong than because "fully developed" implies a finished state. Her imaging studies show that while some brain regions stop growing by the mid-twenties, the connections among regions continue to be reorganized throughout life in response to new skills and experiences. Development, Park suggests, is better understood as ongoing change than as a final product.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Park's research shows that brain regions keep growing larger throughout life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Park argues that brain development actually ends in adolescence rather than early adulthood.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Park's research shows that people learn new skills most easily in their mid-twenties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Park argues that because the brain keeps reorganizing throughout life, calling it fully developed by early adulthood gives a misleading picture.

content.explanation: Park's objection is to the idea of a finished brain. Her studies show connections among brain regions keep reorganizing throughout life, so she sees development as ongoing. Choice D states that main point.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says some regions stop growing by the mid-twenties; what continues is the reorganization of connections.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Park doesn't move the endpoint earlier; she questions whether there is an endpoint at all.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says new skills cause reorganization throughout life but doesn't say when learning is easiest.

passages.text: In the 1950s, some scholars argued that the islands of Polynesia were settled largely by accident, as canoes blown off course drifted to new shores. Later work challenged this view. Computer simulations of drifting canoes found that drift alone was very unlikely to carry voyagers to distant islands such as Hawaii and New Zealand. And in 1976, the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using traditional navigation methods, without instruments, showing that deliberate long-distance voyages were possible.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evidence from computer simulations and a modern voyage undermined the view that Polynesia was settled mainly through accidental drift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computer simulations proved that no drifting canoe could ever have reached Hawaii.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The voyage of Hōkūleʻa showed that the first settlers of Hawaii came from Tahiti.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modern voyagers have retraced every route used by the first settlers of Polynesia.

content.explanation: The text presents an older view (accidental settlement by drift) and then two pieces of evidence that "challenged this view": simulations showing drift was very unlikely to reach distant islands, and a modern voyage showing deliberate navigation was possible. Choice A sums up this main idea.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This overstates the text, which says drift was "very unlikely" to reach such islands, not impossible; it's also just one detail.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The voyage showed that deliberate voyages were possible, not where Hawaii's first settlers came from.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text describes one modern voyage, not the retracing of every route.

passages.text: When Larkfield College opened a new quadrangle in 1998, its planners did something unusual: they planted grass across the entire space and built no sidewalks at all. For the first year, students crossed the lawn however they liked, and their footsteps gradually wore bare trails into the grass. The following summer, the planners paved those trails, turning them into the quad's permanent walkways. Today the paths curve and branch in ways no drafting table would have produced, yet people almost never step off them. On other parts of campus, by contrast, neatly planned sidewalks are lined with muddy shortcuts.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The quadrangle at Larkfield College cost less to build than other parts of the campus because it was built without sidewalks at first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Larkfield's planners based the quadrangle's walkways on the routes people actually took, and those walkways have served walkers better than conventionally planned sidewalks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students at Larkfield College generally prefer walking on grass to walking on paved paths.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The walkways in Larkfield College's quadrangle follow curving and branching routes.

content.explanation: The text describes how the planners let students wear trails into the grass for a year and then paved those trails. It then says people "almost never step off" these paths, while the planned sidewalks elsewhere have "muddy shortcuts" beside them. Together, these points show the main idea: the walkways were based on where people really walked, and they work better than sidewalks drawn up in advance. Choice B states this.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text never mentions cost, so this is not supported, let alone the main idea.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says people almost never leave the paved paths in the quadrangle, so it does not suggest that students prefer grass. The muddy shortcuts elsewhere show they prefer direct routes, not grass.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This detail is in the text, but it is only one feature of the walkways. It leaves out how the walkways were created and why they work, which is the point of the text.

passages.text: In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, people searching for wild honey have an unusual partner: a bird called the greater honeyguide. The bird flies ahead of the honey hunters, calling and stopping on branches, until it reaches a tree that holds a bees' nest. The people then use smoke to calm the bees and cut the nest open. choices.label: B
choices.text: A safe place to perch while it calls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smoke that drives away the bird's predators

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beeswax from nests that the hunters open

distractorRationales.label: B

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The smoke is used to calm the bees so the people can open the nest. The text never says it protects the bird from predators.

passages.text: Accounts of how standard time zones came to the United States usually center on the railroads. Before 1883, towns set their clocks by the local position of the sun, so noon in one city could arrive several minutes before noon in a city just to the west, a confusion that made train schedules hard to follow. Historian Clara Venn does not dispute this account, but she argues that it stops too soon. Once railroad time was adopted, she points out, factories, schools and even churches began to open at hours fixed by distant agreement rather than by daylight. In her view, the railroads' solution to a narrow scheduling problem quietly changed how ordinary people fit their days to the natural world.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Venn accepts the usual explanation of why standard time was adopted but argues that its effects reached well beyond the railroads, changing how people organized their daily lives.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Venn argues that railroads were not actually responsible for the adoption of standard time zones in the United States.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before 1883, differences in local time from one town to the next made train schedules difficult to follow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Venn argues that the adoption of standard time mattered more to factories, schools and churches than it did to the railroads that introduced it.

content.explanation: The text first gives the usual account (railroads needed standard time to make schedules work). It then says Venn "does not dispute this account" but thinks it "stops too soon," because standard time also changed when factories, schools and churches opened, and so changed how people fit their days to the natural world. Choice A captures both parts: she accepts the explanation and argues the effects went far beyond the railroads.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says Venn "does not dispute" the railroad account, so she does not deny that railroads were responsible.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is a supporting detail from the text's background, not the main idea, and it leaves out Venn's argument entirely.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Venn says the effects reached beyond the railroads, but she never compares how much standard time mattered to each group. Saying it mattered more to factories and schools than to railroads overstates her claim.

passages.text: Visitors to the Harlow Museum often remark that the sky in Pieter Vaneck's 1680 landscape looks strangely gray for a summer afternoon. For years, curators assumed that Vaneck had simply painted an overcast day. A recent analysis suggests otherwise. Tiny samples taken from the sky contained smalt, a blue pigment made from ground cobalt glass that was popular at the time and that is known to lose its color over centuries. Under the microscope, the smalt particles nearest the painting's surface had turned grayish, while a few particles sealed deep within the paint layer were still bright blue.

content.stem: According to the text, what did the analysis reveal about the smalt in Vaneck's painting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It had been mixed with a gray pigment to create an overcast sky.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It had faded by the same amount throughout the paint layer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Particles near the surface had faded, but some particles deep in the paint layer had kept their blue color.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It had been added to the painting by a later restorer.

content.explanation: The last sentence reports what the microscope showed: the smalt particles "nearest the painting's surface had turned grayish, while a few particles sealed deep within the paint layer were still bright blue." Choice C restates this. This finding is why the analysis suggests the sky was once blue.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text never mentions a gray pigment. The analysis actually suggests the gray look comes from faded blue smalt, not from Vaneck painting an overcast sky.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says the fading was uneven: particles at the surface turned gray, but some deep particles stayed blue.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says smalt was popular in Vaneck's own time and does not mention any restorer.

passages.text: Most liquids become denser as they cool, and their solid forms sink. Water behaves differently. As a lake cools in autumn, its water grows denser until it reaches about 4°C, and that dense water sinks to the bottom. Water colder than that becomes lighter, so it stays near the surface, where it eventually freezes. The ice floats and acts like a lid, slowing the loss of heat from the water below. As a result, many lakes never freeze solid, and fish can survive the winter in the liquid water near the bottom.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fish survive the winter by swimming to the bottom of lakes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An unusual property of water causes lakes to freeze from the top down, which allows fish to survive beneath the ice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most liquids become denser as they cool.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ice on lakes grows thicker every winter.

content.explanation: The text explains that water, unlike most liquids, becomes lighter once it is colder than about 4°C. Because of this, the coldest water stays at the surface and freezes there, and the floating ice slows heat loss so that the lake does not freeze solid. The text ends with the result: fish survive in the water below. Choice B sums up this whole chain.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text mentions fish living in the water near the bottom, but this is only the final result. It leaves out the main point, which is how water's unusual behavior makes this possible.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is a detail the text uses for contrast. The text's focus is on how water behaves differently from most liquids.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text never says the ice grows thicker every winter.

passages.text: The orchestra's newest violinist, Mei, had practiced the concerto's opening for months, and on the night of the performance she played it exactly as rehearsed: every note in place, every phrase shaped just as her teacher had marked it. Afterward the conductor, a famously sparing man, said only, "Correct." Mei carried the word home like a stone in her pocket. Weeks later, she heard a recording of another violinist playing the same passage with a small, unplanned hesitation before the final note, and she understood at last what the conductor had meant. She felt, to her surprise, grateful rather than wounded.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mei is hurt by the conductor's criticism and decides that she must practice the concerto even harder.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mei discovers that the violinist on the recording is more talented than she is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A remark that at first seems to belittle Mei's performance eventually helps her see that playing every note exactly right was not enough.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conductor of Mei's orchestra rarely praises the musicians who play for him.

content.explanation: Mei plays the opening "exactly as rehearsed," and the conductor says only "Correct." The comparison to a stone in her pocket shows the word weighs on her. Later, hearing another violinist's "small, unplanned hesitation," she understands what the conductor meant: her performance was accurate but lacked that kind of spontaneous life. She ends up grateful. Choice C captures this movement from hurt to understanding.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Mei is hurt at first, but the text never says she decides to practice harder. More practice would also miss the point she comes to understand, since her problem was not mistakes. This choice also ignores her later gratitude.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The recording helps Mei understand the conductor's remark, but the text never says the other violinist is more talented. This overstates the text.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text calls the conductor "famously sparing," but this is a detail about him, not the main idea of a passage centered on what Mei learns.

passages.text: When the Corvale Art Museum dropped its \$15 admission fee in 2019, attendance rose by nearly 40 percent within a year. Museum leaders celebrated, believing they had opened the museum to people who had been kept away by the cost. But a visitor survey conducted by economist Ruth Adeyemi complicated that story. Most of the added visits, she found, came from people who had visited before the change and now simply came more often, sometimes dropping in for only twenty minutes. The share of visitors who were coming for the first time was nearly unchanged.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although dropping the admission fee increased the museum's attendance, the increase came mostly from returning visitors rather than from new audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dropping the admission fee caused fewer people to visit the museum for the first time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museum leaders dropped the admission fee mainly to encourage visitors to make shorter visits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adeyemi's survey shows that a \$15 admission fee is too expensive for most museum visitors.

content.explanation: Attendance rose about 40 percent after the fee was dropped, and leaders thought new people were coming. Adeyemi's survey "complicated that story": most added visits came from people who had already visited and now came more often, and the share of first-time visitors was nearly unchanged. Choice A states this main point.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says the share of first-time visitors was "nearly unchanged," not that first-time visits fell.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says some returning visitors made short visits, but this was a result Adeyemi observed, not the leaders' reason for dropping the fee. The leaders hoped to bring in people kept away by the cost.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The survey found that dropping the fee did not change who visited much, so it does not show that the fee was too expensive for most visitors.

passages.text: The public library in the town of Ferris Bend lends more than books. Since 2017, it has run a seed library: a wooden cabinet of small envelopes holding seeds for beans, tomatoes, squash and wildflowers. Patrons may take up to five envelopes each spring at no cost. In return, the library asks them to let a few of their healthiest plants go to seed in the fall and to bring some of those seeds back, so that the cabinet can be restocked for the following year.

content.stem: According to the text, what does the library ask patrons to do in return for the seeds they take?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pay a small fee each spring

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grow only beans, tomatoes, squash and wildflowers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bring back some seeds from their healthiest plants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Donate books to the library's collection

content.explanation: The last sentence says that in return, the library asks patrons to let some of their healthiest plants go to seed and "to bring some of those seeds back." That is choice C.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says patrons take the seeds "at no cost," so there is no fee.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: These are the kinds of seeds the cabinet holds, but the text does not say patrons may grow only these plants.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says the library lends books but never asks patrons to donate them.

passages.text: Desert ants of the genus Cataglyphis forage far from their nests across flat, featureless sand, yet they return home in a nearly straight line. Scientists suspected that the ants keep track of distance by counting their steps. To test this, researchers glued tiny stilts onto the legs of some ants that had just walked to a feeder, lengthening their stride, and trimmed the legs of others, shortening it. On the trip home, ants on stilts walked past their nest, while ants with shortened legs stopped before reaching it. The ants had apparently taken the expected number of steps, but each step now covered a different distance.

content.stem: Based on the text, why did the ants on stilts walk past their nest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stilts made it harder for them to see landmarks near the nest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They moved faster on stilts and so had less time to notice the nest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They lost count of their steps while walking on stilts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They took about as many steps as usual, but each step was longer than before.

content.explanation: The stilts lengthened the ants' stride. The last sentence explains the result: the ants "had apparently taken the expected number of steps, but each step now covered a different distance." For ants on stilts, each step was longer, so the same number of steps carried them past the nest. That is choice D.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text describes the sand as "featureless" and never mentions landmarks or the ants' vision.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says nothing about speed or about the ants having time to notice the nest.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says the opposite: the ants apparently took the expected number of steps, so they did not lose count.

passages.text: Scientific journals have long favored studies that report a new effect over studies that find none. Many researchers criticize this bias because it hides failed attempts, so others waste time repeating them. Sociologist Anika Solberg agrees but argues that the deeper cost is less obvious. Because a published result is rarely followed by reports of failed attempts to reproduce it, she notes, readers cannot tell a finding that has been confirmed many times from one that has quietly failed every later test. The bias, in her view, distorts not only what scientists choose to study next but also how confident anyone can be in what is already in print.

content.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Solberg argues that researchers waste time because journals rarely publish studies that find no effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Solberg contends that journals' preference for studies reporting new effects also makes it hard to judge how reliable already-published findings are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solberg claims that most published scientific findings fail when other researchers try to reproduce them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Solberg argues that journals should stop publishing studies that report new effects.

content.explanation: The text begins with a common criticism of journals' bias (it wastes researchers' time). Solberg "agrees but argues that the deeper cost is less obvious": since failed attempts to reproduce a result are rarely published, readers cannot tell well-confirmed findings from ones that have failed later tests. So the bias also weakens confidence in what is already in print. Choice B states this main point.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is the common criticism that Solberg agrees with, but the text presents it as background. Her own main point is the "deeper cost" to judging published findings.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Solberg says readers cannot tell which findings have failed later tests. She does not claim that most findings fail, so this overstates her argument.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Solberg criticizes the imbalance in what gets published, but she never suggests that journals stop publishing studies that report new effects.
